\chapter{Months}
\label{ch:ar-months}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the months in Arabic and tell the borrowed civil calendar apart from the Islamic one.}

Say the Latin-sounding civil months, then the first Hijri months, and state what each calendar is used for.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{يناير} \ar{فبراير} \ar{مارس} \ar{أبريل} \ar{مايو} \ar{يونيو} …]{\ar{يناير} to \ar{ديسمبر} — Latin names, borrowed whole, running beside a second calendar}

\label{lesson:AR-C14-ashhur}



\begin{quote}
Here's a genuinely different kind of honesty this lesson needs: Arabic doesn't have \textbf{one} answer to \textquotedblleft{}what are the months called\textquotedblright{} — it has \textbf{two full calendars}, used for different purposes, side by side.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Gregorian months}
For the everyday, civil, solar calendar, Modern Standard Arabic simply \textbf{borrows} the familiar Latin-derived month names you already know from Spanish/French/English:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{$\approx$} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{يناير}} (\emph{yanāyir}) & January \\
\textbf{\ar{فبراير}} (\emph{fabrāyir}) & February \\
\textbf{\ar{مارس}} (\emph{māris}) & March \\
\textbf{\ar{أبريل}} (\emph{abrīl}) & April \\
\textbf{\ar{مايو}} (\emph{māyū}) & May \\
\textbf{\ar{يونيو}} (\emph{yūniyū}) & June \\
\textbf{\ar{يوليو}} (\emph{yūliyū}) & July \\
\textbf{\ar{أغسطس}} (\emph{aghusṭus}) & August \\
\textbf{\ar{سبتمبر}} (\emph{sibtambir}) & September \\
\textbf{\ar{أكتوبر}} (\emph{uktūbar}) & October \\
\textbf{\ar{نوفمبر}} (\emph{nūfambir}) & November \\
\textbf{\ar{ديسمبر}} (\emph{dīsambir}) & December \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You can hear the Latin (and French) originals right through the Arabic sounds — this is a straightforward, recent borrowing for civil/business use, not an ancient Arabic-invented system.

\textbf{One more honest wrinkle:} these Latin-derived names are the everyday convention in Egypt, the Gulf, and much pan-Arab media — but the Levant and Iraq (Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine, Iraq) traditionally use a \textbf{third}, completely different set for these same twelve solar months, of \textbf{Syriac} origin: \textbf{\ar{كانون} \ar{الثاني}} (\emph{Kānūn al-Thānī}, January), \textbf{\ar{شباط}} (\emph{Shubāṭ}, February), \textbf{\ar{آذار}} (\emph{Ādhār}, March), and so on. So depending on the country, an Arabic speaker's civil-calendar month name might come from Latin \emph{or} from Syriac — a third naming system, not just two.

\begin{culture}
For \textbf{religious life} — Ramadan, Hajj, and the Islamic calendar generally — Arabic uses an entirely \textbf{separate} set of month names, from the \textbf{lunar Hijri calendar}: \textbf{\ar{محرم}} (\emph{Muḥarram}), \textbf{\ar{صفر}} (\emph{Ṣafar}), \textbf{\ar{ربيع} \ar{الأول}/\ar{الثاني}} (\emph{Rabīʿ al-Awwal/al-Thānī} — the very \textquotedblleft{}Rabīʿ\textquotedblright{} from the seasons lesson), and eight more, none of which correspond to a fixed solar month. Because the Hijri calendar has \textbf{no leap-month correction}, these twelve lunar months drift steadily across all four solar seasons over a roughly 33-year cycle — so Ramadan, for instance, doesn't fall in the same season every year.

Two calendars, two jobs: the borrowed Latin names for the ordinary business week, the older lunar names for religious observance.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}yanāyir, fabrāyir, māris\textquotedblright{} — January, February, March — hear the Latin
  \item the second calendar — \textquotedblleft{}Muḥarram, Ṣafar, Rabīʿ al-Awwal\textquotedblright{} — entirely different names
  \item the honest point — two calendars, two purposes, both in everyday use
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where do Arabic's civil month names (\emph{yanāyir, māris...}) come from? (\textbf{Borrowed Latin/European names}, recent civil-calendar loans.) What runs alongside them for religious life? (\textbf{The Hijri lunar calendar}, with its own entirely different 12 month names — \emph{Muḥarram, Ṣafar, Rabīʿ al-Awwal}...) Why do Hijri months drift across the seasons? (\textbf{No leap-month correction} — the lunar year is shorter than the solar year, so the calendar drifts over a \textasciitilde{}33-year cycle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
